consensus_summary: Mainstream consensus reads 'shadow of death' as the deepest darkness and gloom of mortal peril or death itself—an extremity of danger, suffering, or the realm of the dead—through which God's presence protects the believer (Psalm 23:4), extended in the prophetic/NT strand (Isa 9:2; Matt 4:16; Luke 1:79) to the spiritual darkness of humanity apart from God, dispelled by the light of Christ. A live philological alternative treats the Hebrew as simply 'deep darkness.'
book_summary: The book defines a shadow as the image, outline, or boundary of its subject, so the Shadow of Death is specifically the boundary of Death's mountain-kingdom. The valley of Psalm 23 is the low border passage between two mountain-kingdoms, through which the Shepherd leads His people out of Death's kingdom of darkness into Christ's kingdom of light and life. It is paired with an explicit opposite, the Shadow of Christ.
consensus_core_identification: The shadow of death = the darkest extremity of mortal peril, dying, or the domain of death (and, derivatively, spiritual darkness apart from God), through which God accompanies and from which Christ's light delivers.
book_core_identification: The shadow of death = the territorial boundary/outline of Death's kingdom, with the valley as the border passage through which God's people are transferred from Death's kingdom into Christ's kingdom.
boundary_disagreement: The consensus treats the phrase as a broad poetic image covering mortal danger, the experience of dying, Sheol, gloom, oppression, and spiritual darkness. The book narrows it to one precise structural referent—the boundary line of Death's kingdom—and reclassifies Psalm 23:4 from 'peril traversed under God's protection' to 'border crossing between two kingdoms.' It thereby excludes (or at least deprioritizes) readings such as generic deep darkness, mortal peril per se, deathbed experience, or despair, while adding a systematic opposite ('Shadow of Christ') absent from all consensus accounts.
material_contradiction: None strictly. The book's boundary-of-Death's-kingdom reading is a spatial-systematic sharpening of the consensus's quasi-locative 'realm of the dead' alternative and its Christ-dispels-darkness strand (Col 1:13 kingdom transfer). Both can be true of the same referent; the book does not deny that the shadow concerns death, darkness, or deliverance into Christ's light.
rationale: The book preserves the consensus's central category—death's dark domain from which God delivers into Christ's light—but materially changes its precision and extension. It converts a diffuse poetic image into a technical term ('shadow' = boundary/outline; 'valley' = pass between mountain-kingdoms), reclassifies Psalm 23:4 as a border transit rather than protected peril, and imports the Daniel 2 mountain-as-kingdom scheme and 1 Sam 17:3 valley geography that no consensus response invokes. This is a real boundary-level disagreement (which cases the symbol covers and what mechanism it names) without replacing the referent, since the deliverance-from-darkness-into-Christ's-kingdom reading (Ps 107; Isa 9:2; Luke 1:79; Col 1:13) is a recognized consensus strand. Hence REFINED, not DIVERGENT or NOVEL.
strongest_objection: One could argue NOVEL: no consensus response or alternative identifies the shadow as a 'boundary of a kingdom' or posits an opposing 'Shadow of Christ,' and the definitional move (shadow = outline/boundary) is an interpretive system foreign to all listed readings. The cited verses establish valley-between-mountains and mountain-as-kingdom separately, but no printed text states that a shadow marks a kingdom's boundary—the core claim rests on inference across chapters rather than direct textual support, which could also push toward NOVEL rather than REFINED.
